a1-arraylist.summary: Java's Collections Framework gives you ready-made lists, sets, maps, queues and heaps. You will learn how each one works inside, what every common operation costs, and how to choose the right one from the question your algorithm keeps asking — the skill behind almost every efficient interview solution.

a1-big-o.summary: Big-O notation is the precise language for describing how fast a cost grows, with constant factors and small terms deliberately removed. You will learn what O, Ω and Θ actually claim, how to simplify any cost expression correctly, how to read common recurrences, and when an asymptotic ranking can mislead you on real inputs.

a1-comparable-comparator.summary: Sorting, TreeMap, TreeSet and PriorityQueue all depend on one question — which of two objects comes first? You will learn how Java's Comparable and Comparator answer it, how to write comparisons that are correct for every input, and why a wrong comparator silently breaks sorts, trees and heaps.

a1-custom-classes.summary: Small custom types — a grid cell, an edge, an interval, a tree or trie node — make solutions readable and are required whenever an object becomes a map key or a heap element. You will learn when to write one, how records and static nested classes work, and the equals/hashCode and ordering rules that decide whether collections treat your objects correctly.

a1-java-streams-interviews.summary: Java streams describe a computation over a collection as a pipeline of steps — filter, transform, group, collect — instead of a hand-written loop. You will learn how a pipeline actually executes, the handful of operations and collectors that cover most interview tasks, what streams cost, and when a plain loop is the better choice.

a1-java-syntax-competitive.summary: The small slice of Java you need to solve problems on an online judge or in a coding interview — the program skeleton, reading input, choosing int or long, printing efficiently and doing arithmetic modulo a prime. Getting these right means your time goes into the algorithm instead of fighting the language.

a1-recursion.summary: Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller copies of the same problem until one is small enough to answer directly. You will learn how to design a recursive method, what the call stack does while it runs, how to analyse its time and space, and how the same idea grows into tree traversal, backtracking and memoized dynamic programming.

a1-strings-stringbuilder.summary: Java strings cannot be changed after they are created, which makes them safe to share and hash but turns careless concatenation in a loop into an O(n²) bug. You will learn how String and StringBuilder work, how to read, compare and build text correctly, and the counting and two-pointer techniques behind most string interview problems.

a1-time-complexity.summary: Time complexity describes how the number of steps an algorithm performs grows as its input grows, and space complexity does the same for the extra memory it uses. You will learn to count both from code, account for hidden library costs, and use a problem's constraints to decide which solutions can possibly pass before you write them.

a10-heap-greedy.summary: Some greedy algorithms need "the best item right now" while the set of items keeps changing — merged results re-enter the pool, new options unlock over time, or an earlier choice turns out to be a mistake. You will learn the three shapes of heap-based greedy (combine the smallest, unlock then choose, commit then regret), why a priority queue makes each step O(log n), and how to prove these greedy choices correct.

a10-interval-scheduling.summary: Interval scheduling is the family of greedy problems where requests occupy a stretch of time on a shared resource and you must choose, assign or cover them optimally. You will learn why "earliest finish first" keeps the most requests, how to prove it two different ways, how the same reasoning gives the fewest rooms and the fewest covering intervals, and why adding weights breaks greedy and calls for dynamic programming.

a10-local-vs-global.summary: A greedy algorithm takes the locally best step and never looks back; this lesson is about deciding whether those local steps add up to the globally best answer. You will learn the two properties that make greedy correct, three proof techniques, how to hunt for counterexamples systematically, and what to do when greedy fails — with coin change, knapsack, Jump Game and Gas Station as worked cases.

a10-sorting-greedy.summary: Many optimisation problems become a single pass once the items are in the right order — the hard part is finding that order and proving it is right. You will learn to derive a sort key with the adjacent-swap argument, apply it to scheduling, matching, ratio and cost-difference problems, and recognise when a sort-then-scan greedy is safe and when it is not.

a11-1d-dp.summary: One-dimensional DP solves problems whose subproblems are named by a single number — a prefix length, a position, or an amount. You will derive House Robber, Decode Ways, Coin Change and Word Break from their brute-force recursions, learn the four common shapes of a one-index state, and reduce the memory to a couple of variables where the recurrence allows it.

a11-2d-dp.summary: Some problems cannot be described by one index, because the answer depends on two things at once — positions in two strings, a row and a column, or an item and a remaining capacity. You will learn how to spot the second dimension, derive a two-index recurrence from the choices in the problem, pick a fill order from the dependency arrows, and shrink the table to one or two rows.

a11-bitmask-dp.summary: Bitmask DP is dynamic programming whose state includes a subset of a small set of items, stored as the bits of an integer. You will learn when the subset really must be part of the state, how to encode and iterate subsets in Java, and how to derive the travelling-salesman (Held–Karp), assignment and submask-partition recurrences, with their O(2ⁿ) costs and the n ≤ 20 rule of thumb.

a11-grid-dp.summary: Grid DP solves counting and optimisation problems on a matrix by asking how you could have arrived at each cell. You will derive the state, recurrence, base cases and fill direction for path counting, minimum cost, obstacles, backward-computed constraints, squares and two simultaneous walkers, and learn to tell when a grid is not a DP at all.

a11-knapsack.summary: Knapsack problems ask you to choose items under a capacity limit, and a surprising number of interview problems are knapsacks in disguise. You will derive the 0/1 knapsack DP from a take-or-skip recursion, compress it to one array and prove why the loop direction matters, and then adapt the same state to unbounded items, subset sum, counting problems and limited copies.

a11-lcs.summary: The longest common subsequence of two strings is the longest sequence of characters that appears in both, in the same order, with gaps allowed. You will derive its dynamic-programming solution from first principles by asking what can happen to the last character of each string, then reconstruct the sequence, cut memory to one row, and reuse the same reasoning for edit distance, supersequences and palindromes.

a11-lis.summary: The longest increasing subsequence (LIS) is the longest run of values you can pick from an array, in their original order, so that each one is larger than the last. You will derive the O(n²) dynamic programming solution from a brute-force recursion, then derive the O(n log n) "tails" algorithm, prove why it works, and adapt both to the variants interviews ask for.

a11-memoization.summary: Dynamic programming makes slow recursive searches fast by solving each distinct subproblem once. You will learn to spot repeated work, derive a DP from a problem through five decisions — state, recurrence, base cases, order of computation and answer — and implement it either top-down with memoization or bottom-up with tabulation, knowing when each is the better choice.

a11-partition-dp.summary: Partition DP solves problems that ask you to cut a sequence into pieces as well as possible. You will learn its two shapes — choosing the last piece of a prefix, and choosing the split point of an interval — and derive the state, recurrence, base cases and fill order for palindrome cuts, bounded pieces, k-way splits, matrix chains and Burst Balloons.

a11-state-machine-dp.summary: State-machine DP handles sequences where your options at each step depend on a small "mode" you are in — holding a stock or not, in cooldown, how many transactions are left. You will learn to draw the modes and legal transitions first, turn the drawing into one DP value per mode per step, and solve the whole Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock family plus non-stock problems with the same method.

a11-subsequences.summary: Subsequence problems ask you to pick elements in their original order while skipping any you like. You will learn why brute force over subsequences is exponential, how to choose among the four standard dynamic programming states for these problems, and how to derive solutions for matching, counting and palindrome questions from first principles.

a11-tree-dp.summary: DP on trees computes an answer for every subtree from the answers of its children, in one post-order pass. You will learn to design the small summary each node reports to its parent, derive multi-state recurrences such as rob/skip and the three camera states, run tree DP on adjacency lists without recursion, and answer a question for every possible root with rerooting.

a12-fenwick.summary: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) keeps prefix sums of a changing array in a single array of n + 1 numbers, answering prefix sums and point updates in O(log n) with a few lines of code. You will learn what each cell stores, why `i & -i` drives both loops, and how to extend it to range updates, inversion counting and order statistics.

a12-prefix-matching.summary: Prefix matching covers two related jobs — finding which stored words are prefixes of (or start with) a query, and finding where a pattern occurs in a long text without re-reading characters. You will learn trie-based longest/shortest prefix matching and top-k suggestions, then KMP's prefix function, the Z-function and Rabin-Karp rolling hashes.

a12-segment-trees.summary: A segment tree stores aggregates (sums, minimums, maximums and more) of every half, quarter and smaller piece of an array, so that range queries and updates both take O(log n). You will learn how it is built, why a query touches only O(log n) nodes, how to support any associative operation, and how lazy propagation makes range updates fast.

a12-sparse-tables.summary: A sparse table precomputes the answer for every power-of-two-length window of a fixed array, so that range minimum, maximum, GCD, AND and OR queries take O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. You will learn how it is built, why two overlapping blocks are enough, which operations allow that overlap, and when to choose it over a segment tree.

a12-trie.summary: A trie stores a set of strings as a tree of characters, so that every prefix of every word is a single node you can walk to in O(L) time. You will learn how insert, search and prefix queries work, how to count, delete and list words, and how the same structure solves wildcard search, autocomplete and maximum-XOR problems.

a13-and-or-xor.summary: AND, OR and XOR combine two integers one binary digit at a time. You will learn how Java stores integers in two's complement, what each bitwise operator (and NOT and the shifts) does to those bits, and the handful of algebraic facts that turn up in almost every bit-manipulation problem.

a13-bitmasking.summary: A bitmask stores a subset of a small set of items as the bits of one integer, so set operations become single instructions and every subset can be listed by counting. You will learn to encode sets, enumerate all subsets, submasks and fixed-size subsets, recognise the n ≤ 20 signal, and see how masks become the state of a dynamic program.

a13-powers-of-two.summary: A power of two is a number with exactly one bit set, and that one fact gives O(1) tests, fast rounding, cheap modulo and integer logarithms. You will learn why n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 works, how to round to the neighbouring powers of two, and why hash tables and many data structures size themselves in powers of two.

a13-set-bit.summary: Setting, clearing, toggling and testing a single bit are the four basic moves of bit manipulation. You will learn to build the one-bit mask `1 << k`, why each move uses the operator it does, the lowest-set-bit tricks `n & (n - 1)` and `n & -n`, and the overflow and precedence traps that break these one-liners in Java.

a13-xor-tricks.summary: XOR cancels equal values, so a whole array can be folded into one number in which every paired element has disappeared. You will learn the algebra behind that, and use it to solve Single Number I, II and III, Missing Number, range XOR and subarray-XOR counting in linear time with constant or small extra space.

a14-brute-force-first.summary: Before optimising, a strong candidate states the simplest correct solution and its exact cost. You will learn how to find the brute force for any problem by naming its candidate space, how to state its complexity honestly, how to present it in under two minutes, and how it becomes both the starting point for optimisation and a trusted test oracle.

a14-clarifying-requirements.summary: Interview problems are deliberately underspecified, and the first few minutes decide whether you solve the problem that was asked. You will learn which questions change the algorithm or the output, how to confirm the answers with examples, and what to do when the interviewer will not answer.

a14-clean-coding.summary: Interview code is usually written without autocomplete, error highlighting or a run button, and it is read by someone deciding whether they want to work with you. You will learn to structure code before filling it in, name and decompose it so it can be traced by hand, write the Java APIs you need from memory, and avoid the bugs a compiler will not catch for you.

a14-complexity-in-interview.summary: Every interview solution ends with "what is the time and space complexity?", and a wrong answer there undoes a lot of good work. You will learn a repeatable method for analysing your own code under pressure — naming variables, counting iterations rather than loops, catching hidden library costs and recursion stack space — and how to state the result in a few clear sentences.

a14-deriving-optimization.summary: Interviewers care less about whether you know the optimal solution than whether you can get there from a slow one. You will learn a repeatable way to do it — use the constraints to set a target, find the work the brute force repeats, pick the technique that removes exactly that work, and check the idea against a counterexample before coding.

a14-edge-cases.summary: Most interview solutions that fail do so on an input the candidate never thought about — an empty array, a single node, a zero, a value at the edge of the integer range. You will learn a systematic way to generate those inputs, how to find the ones that threaten your specific code by reading its branches, and when in the interview to raise them.

a14-manual-testing.summary: In most coding interviews there is no test runner and no debugger, so you verify code by executing it in your head. You will learn how to choose a handful of inputs that expose bugs, compute their expected answers independently, trace loops and recursion with a variable table, and fix what you find without breaking what already worked.

a14-responding-to-hints.summary: Interviewers give hints all the time — as questions, suggestions or gentle warnings — and how you respond is part of what they assess. You will learn to recognise the different kinds of hint and what each usually means, a five-step way to take one on board visibly, how to push back politely when you think a hint does not apply, and when and how to ask for a hint yourself.

a14-thinking-aloud.summary: In a live coding interview, the interviewer can only grade the reasoning they can hear. You will learn what to say in each phase of a problem, how to narrate code without slowing down, how to think aloud productively when stuck, and you will follow a complete annotated interview on a heap-based interval problem.

a14-timed-coding.summary: Real coding interviews give you roughly 35–45 minutes per problem, and running out of time with no working code is one of the most common ways to fail. You will learn how to budget an interview session, which checkpoints tell you to change course, what to cut when time is short, and how to build timed stamina through solo timed practice and mock interviews.

a2-array-string-traversal.summary: Almost every array and string problem is solved by walking the data in a deliberate order while keeping a little state. You will learn the core traversal patterns — single pass, backward pass, read/write compaction, reversal and parse-while-scanning — and how to choose between them so your solutions stay O(n).

a2-difference-arrays.summary: A difference array stores how much each element differs from the one before it, so adding a value to a whole range touches only two entries. You will learn why that works, how to apply thousands of range updates in O(1) each and rebuild the array with one prefix-sum pass, how to handle 1-based and half-open ranges, and when to switch to a sweep, a 2D grid version or a Fenwick tree.

a2-frequency-counting.summary: Frequency counting answers "how many of each?" by tallying elements into an array or hash map in one pass, which turns comparisons that would otherwise need sorting or nested loops into O(n) work. You will learn how to choose the counting container, the standard counting idioms in Java, and the classic problems built on them — anagrams, first unique character, grouping, top-k and majority voting.

a2-hashing.summary: Hashing lets a program answer "have I seen this before?" and "where did I see it?" in constant average time, which turns many O(n²) search problems into a single O(n) pass. You will learn how a hash table works inside Java's HashMap, what makes a good key, and the core hashing patterns — membership, complement lookup, last-seen index, prefix sums with counts and sequence building.

a2-intervals.summary: Interval problems work with ranges such as meetings, bookings and IP blocks, asking whether they overlap, how to merge them, how many can fit, and how many run at once. You will learn the overlap test, why sorting by start or by end turns quadratic pair checks into one linear pass, and the handful of techniques — merge, insert, intersect, greedy selection and sweep — that cover almost every interval question.

a2-kadane.summary: Kadane's algorithm finds the contiguous subarray with the largest sum in a single pass, by asking at every index whether to extend the best run that ends there or start a new one. You will derive it from brute force, prove why the one-line recurrence is correct, handle the all-negative and empty-subarray cases, and adapt it to circular arrays, products, stock prices and 2D grids.

a2-matrix.summary: A matrix is a grid of rows and columns, and grid problems — images, game boards, maps, spreadsheets — reward a small set of skills used precisely. You will learn how Java stores 2D arrays, how to traverse them in every common order, how to transform them in place, how to search sorted grids faster than cell by cell, and how to treat a grid as a graph for flood fill.

a2-prefix-suffix.summary: Prefix and suffix techniques precompute what lies to the left and to the right of every index in one or two linear passes, so questions that would need a fresh scan for each index — range sums, "everything except me", water trapped between walls — are answered in O(1) each. You will learn to build these tables, combine them correctly at the boundaries, and recognise when a problem is asking for them.

a2-sliding-window.summary: A sliding window keeps a contiguous range of an array or string and updates a small summary of it as the range moves, so you can find the best subarray or substring under a constraint in O(n) instead of checking all O(n²) ranges. You will learn fixed and variable windows, the monotonicity condition that makes shrinking safe, and the standard variations interviewers build on.

a2-sorting-based.summary: Many array problems become easy once the data is in order — duplicates sit next to each other, the closest values become neighbours, and a greedy choice or a two-pointer scan becomes provably correct. You will learn what sorting buys you, what it costs, how to choose the sort key, and how to recognise "sort first, then scan" problems.

a2-two-pointers.summary: The two-pointer technique keeps two indices into a sequence and moves them by a rule that provably discards impossible candidates, turning many O(n²) pair-checking problems into a single O(n) pass. You will learn the three families — converging, same-direction and two-sequence pointers — how to prove each move is safe, and how to recognise the pattern in new problems.

a3-binary-search-on-answer.summary: Binary search on the answer solves "find the smallest (or largest) value that works" problems by guessing a value, checking whether it works, and halving the range of guesses. You will learn to spot these problems, prove the monotonic property they rely on, write the feasibility check, and get the search boundaries right for both minimising and maximising.

a3-binary-search.summary: Binary search finds a value in sorted data by discarding half of the remaining candidates with every comparison. You will learn why sorted order makes that possible, how to write the loop so it is provably correct, and how to recognise binary-search problems that do not look like searching at all.

a3-comparator-sorting.summary: Comparator-based sorting lets you sort anything — records, intervals, strings, indices — by rules you define, using the library's O(n log n) sort. You will learn the comparator contract and why breaking it produces wrong results, how to build multi-key orderings safely in Java, and how a well-chosen ordering turns problems such as Largest Number and meeting-room scheduling into a sort plus a scan.

a3-counting-sort.summary: Comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n), but when keys are small integers or spread evenly over a known range, you can sort without comparing at all. You will learn counting sort, its stable prefix-sum form and its use inside radix sort, and bucket sort for evenly distributed values — including when each one is fast and when it breaks down.

a3-lower-upper-bounds.summary: Lower and upper bounds are the binary-search variants that find boundaries instead of matches — the first element at least x, the first element greater than x. You will learn to derive both from one invariant and use them for first and last occurrences, counts, insertion points, floor and ceiling queries.

a3-merge-sort.summary: Merge sort sorts by splitting the data in half, sorting each half, and merging the two sorted halves in one linear pass. You will learn why that gives a guaranteed O(n log n) running time and a stable result, how to implement it on arrays and linked lists, and how its merge step solves problems such as counting inversions.

a3-quick-sort.summary: Quicksort sorts by choosing a pivot, rearranging the array so smaller elements sit left of it and larger ones right, and then sorting each side. You will learn how partitioning works and why it is correct, why the average running time is O(n log n) but the worst case is O(n²), and how random pivots, three-way partitioning and hybrid designs make quicksort fast and safe in practice.

a3-quickselect.summary: Quickselect finds the k-th smallest element of an unsorted array in O(n) average time by partitioning like quicksort but continuing into only one side. You will learn why discarding a side is safe, why the average cost is linear, how to avoid its O(n²) worst case, and when a heap is the better tool.

a4-cycle-detection.summary: A linked list has a cycle when following next pointers never reaches null because some node points back to an earlier one. You will learn to detect a cycle with a hash set and then with Floyd's tortoise-and-hare in O(1) space, to prove why the second phase finds the exact node where the cycle begins, and to spot the same structure hiding in number sequences and arrays.

a4-fast-slow-pointers.summary: Fast/slow pointers walk a linked list with two references moving at different speeds, or with a fixed gap between them, so that one pass reveals positions you could otherwise find only by measuring the list first. You will learn why the technique works, how to get its loop guards exactly right, and how to recognise it in middle-of-list, nth-from-end, palindrome and cycle problems.

a4-intersection.summary: Two singly linked lists intersect when, from some node onwards, they share the very same nodes — a Y shape. You will learn why the shared part must run all the way to the end, how to find the first shared node with a hash set, by aligning lengths, or with the elegant pointer-switching trick, and why the comparison must be on node identity rather than value.

a4-lru-style.summary: An LRU cache keeps a bounded number of entries and, when full, evicts the one used least recently — with every lookup, insert and eviction in O(1). You will learn why neither a hash map nor a list can do this alone, how a hash map pointing into a doubly linked list with sentinels does it, and how the same move-to-front manipulation extends to LinkedHashMap, LFU caches and production cache design.

a4-merge-lists.summary: Merging combines sorted linked lists into one sorted list by repeatedly taking the smaller front node, rewiring existing nodes instead of copying them. You will learn the two-list merge with a dummy and a tail pointer, why it is linear, how to keep it stable, and how to scale it to k lists with a heap or with divide and conquer — plus the array and merge-sort variants built on the same idea.

a4-reversal.summary: Reversing a linked list means turning every next pointer around so the last node becomes the head, using only a few local references. You will learn the iterative three-pointer method and the invariant that makes it correct, the recursive version and its stack cost, and how to reverse only part of a list — the building block behind sublist, k-group, palindrome and reorder problems.

a4-singly-linked-lists.summary: A linked list stores a sequence as a chain of separate nodes joined by references instead of one contiguous block of memory. You will learn how singly and doubly linked lists are built, what each operation really costs, and the pointer habits — save before you rewire, use a dummy node — that make every later linked-list problem manageable.

a5-deque.summary: A deque (double-ended queue) lets you add and remove items at both ends in O(1). You will learn how it is stored as a circular array, how one Java class serves as stack, queue and deque, and the problems — palindromes, 0-1 BFS and sliding windows — where needing both ends is the whole point.

a5-monotonic-queue.summary: A monotonic queue is a deque kept sorted so that the maximum or minimum of a moving window is always at its front. You will learn how it extends the monotonic stack with expiry, why it gives sliding-window extremes in O(n), and how the same idea speeds up dynamic programming and prefix-sum problems.

a5-monotonic-stack.summary: A monotonic stack is an ordinary stack that you keep sorted by popping anything the new element makes useless. You will learn why that single rule answers "nearest larger or smaller element" questions for every index in O(n), how to choose the stack's direction, and how to apply it to histograms, digit removal and subarray-minimum sums.

a5-next-greater-smaller.summary: Next and previous greater or smaller element problems ask, for every position, where the nearest larger or smaller value is. You will learn the four variants, how a monotonic stack answers each in O(n), how to handle ties, circular arrays and online input, and how to recognise these problems behind stories about temperatures and stock prices.

a5-parentheses.summary: Bracket and expression problems are where stacks earn their reputation. You will learn to validate, repair, measure and generate parenthesised strings, and then to evaluate arithmetic expressions — postfix, infix with precedence, parentheses and unary minus — using stacks, the shunting-yard algorithm and recursive descent.

a5-queue.summary: A queue hands items out in the order they arrived — first in, first out. You will learn how queues are stored efficiently, how to use Java's queue API without its traps, how to build a queue from two stacks, and why breadth-first search depends on a queue to find shortest paths.

a5-stack.summary: A stack is a collection where the last item added is the first one removed. You will learn why that single rule makes stacks the natural tool for nesting, undoing and deferring work, how to use one correctly in Java, and how to spot stack problems in interviews.

a6-bfs.summary: Breadth-first search visits a tree one level at a time, using a queue to remember which nodes are waiting. You will learn why a queue produces level order, how to process each level separately, and how to shape the output for level-order, zigzag, bottom-up and per-level summary problems.

a6-binary-trees.summary: A binary tree stores data as a hierarchy in which every node has at most two children. You will learn the vocabulary and shapes of binary trees, how to represent and build them in Java, and the recursive way of thinking that solves almost every tree problem in a few lines.

a6-bst.summary: A binary search tree keeps its keys ordered so that every comparison discards a whole subtree, giving fast search, insertion and deletion on data that keeps changing. You will learn the ordering rule and why it makes inorder traversal sorted, implement every core operation, validate a tree correctly, and see why balance decides whether operations cost O(log n) or O(n).

a6-construction.summary: Tree construction rebuilds a binary tree from a description of it — usually two traversal orders, sometimes one traversal plus an ordering rule. You will learn which descriptions determine a tree uniquely, how preorder and inorder combine to rebuild it in O(n), and the related constructions interviews ask for, from BSTs out of preorder to maximum binary trees with a monotonic stack.

a6-dfs.summary: Depth-first search walks a tree by going as deep as possible along one branch before backing up. You will learn the three depth-first orders, how to pass information down and up a tree, how to collect root-to-leaf paths with backtracking, and how to write every traversal iteratively when recursion is not an option.

a6-diameter.summary: The diameter of a tree is the longest path between any two nodes, and that path need not pass through the root. You will learn to find it in one O(n) pass by returning heights while recording the best path at each node, and to reuse the same pattern for maximum path sum, longest univalue path and diameters of general trees.

a6-height-depth.summary: Height and depth measure how tall a tree is and how far down a node sits, and they decide the cost of nearly every tree operation. You will learn both definitions and their edge-versus-node conventions, compute maximum and minimum depth correctly, and check whether a tree is balanced in a single O(n) pass.

a6-lca.summary: The lowest common ancestor of two nodes is the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree. You will learn the five-line postorder solution and exactly why it works, the variants that interviews build on it (parent pointers, missing nodes, BSTs, distances), and how binary lifting answers many queries in O(log n) each.

a6-nary-trees.summary: An N-ary tree lets each node have any number of children, which is how file systems, the DOM, organisation charts and JSON documents are shaped. You will learn how to represent one in Java, how every binary-tree traversal generalises by looping over children, and how to serialise N-ary trees or convert them to binary trees with the left-child right-sibling trick.

a6-path-problems.summary: Tree path problems ask about sums, counts or sequences along paths, and almost all of them fall into four families depending on where a path may start and end. You will learn to classify a path problem in one question, carry state down for root-to-leaf paths, count downward paths in O(n) with prefix sums, and handle paths that bend or run in any direction.

a6-serialization.summary: Serialisation turns a tree of objects into a flat string or byte sequence that can be stored or sent, and deserialisation rebuilds the identical tree from it. You will learn why null markers make a single preorder sequence enough, how to write and test a codec in both preorder and level-order styles, and how the same encoding solves problems such as finding duplicate subtrees.

a6-tree-views.summary: Tree view problems ask which nodes you would see when looking at a drawn tree from one side — from the right, from above, from below, or column by column. You will learn to give every node a row and a column, and to solve right and left views, top and bottom views, vertical order, boundary traversal and maximum width as small variations of BFS or DFS over those coordinates.

a7-k-way-merge.summary: K-way merge combines k sorted sequences into one sorted sequence by repeatedly taking the smallest of their current front elements. You will learn why a min heap of k fronts does this in O(N log k), what each heap entry must carry, how to merge lazily over streams, and how the same idea solves k-th smallest in a sorted matrix, k smallest pairs and the smallest range covering k lists.

a7-min-heap.summary: A heap keeps the smallest (or largest) element permanently at the front while still allowing fast inserts and removals. You will learn how a min heap and a max heap are laid out in a plain array, how sift-up and sift-down restore order in O(log n), why building a heap from n values takes only O(n), and how to get either kind from Java's PriorityQueue without comparator bugs.

a7-priority-queues.summary: A priority queue hands out the most important waiting item next, not the oldest. You will learn the abstract operations, why a binary heap is the standard implementation, how to design comparators with tie-breakers in Java, how to "change" a priority with lazy deletion, and how to recognise scheduling and best-next problems that a priority queue solves.

a7-running-median.summary: The running median is the middle value of a stream that keeps growing, available after every new number. You will learn why re-sorting is too slow, how splitting the numbers into a max heap of the lower half and a min heap of the upper half gives O(log n) inserts and O(1) median queries, and how to keep the two halves correctly ordered and balanced.

a7-top-k.summary: Top-K problems ask for the k largest, smallest, most frequent or closest items without sorting everything. You will learn why a bounded heap of size k solves them in O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, how to pick the heap's polarity and tie-breaking correctly, and when quickselect or bucket sort is the better tool.

a7-two-heap-pattern.summary: The two-heap pattern uses a pair of heaps when a problem needs fast access to two different extremes at once — the boundary between a lower and an upper group, or the best item among those that a second ordering has made available. You will learn both forms, how to keep them consistent with invariants, how lazy deletion lets them handle sliding windows, and how to recognise the pattern in scheduling problems such as IPO.

a8-articulation-points.summary: An articulation point is a vertex whose removal splits an undirected graph — a single point of failure among the nodes. You will learn how one depth-first search with discovery times and low-link values finds every such vertex in linear time, why the root of the search needs its own rule, how cut vertices relate to bridges, and how the same search splits a graph into biconnected components.

a8-bellman-ford.summary: Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths from one source even when some edges have negative weights, by relaxing every edge V − 1 times, and one more pass tells you whether a negative cycle makes shortest paths meaningless. You will learn why V − 1 passes are enough, how the extra pass detects negative cycles, and how the same relaxation idea solves "at most K edges" and constraint problems.

a8-bfs.summary: Breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS) are the two ways to visit every vertex of a graph, and almost every graph algorithm is built on one of them. You will learn how each works and why, how BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, how to write DFS with and without recursion, how to choose between them, and how to deep-copy a graph — including one with shared nodes.

a8-bipartite.summary: A graph is bipartite when its vertices can be split into two groups so that every edge joins the two groups. You will learn why a simple BFS or DFS 2-colouring decides this in linear time, why a graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle, how to produce that odd cycle as proof, and how the same idea decides whether a graph splits into two cliques.

a8-bridges.summary: A bridge is an edge of an undirected graph whose removal disconnects part of the graph — a single point of failure among the links. You will learn why bridges are exactly the edges on no cycle, how one depth-first search with discovery times and low-link values finds all of them in linear time, and how to apply it to the Critical Connections problem and to network-hardening questions.

a8-connected-components.summary: A connected component is a maximal group of vertices that can all reach one another. You will learn the one pattern that finds every component — an outer loop that starts a BFS or DFS from each unvisited vertex — and apply it to graphs, grids, largest regions, forests, and the sink questions that come up for directed graphs.

a8-cycle-detection.summary: A directed graph has a cycle exactly when depth-first search finds an edge back to a vertex that is still on the current path, or equivalently when repeatedly removing vertices with no incoming edges gets stuck. You will learn both tests, the white/gray/black colour scheme that makes the DFS version precise, how to print the cycle you found, and how Bellman-Ford detects the special case of a cycle whose total weight is negative.

a8-cycle-undirected.summary: An undirected graph has a cycle exactly when some traversal meets an already-visited vertex by an edge other than the one it arrived on. You will learn why the parent check is needed, how to detect cycles with DFS, BFS and Union-Find, and how the same ideas extend to finding the shortest or minimum-weight cycle, counting cycles of a given length and listing every cycle.

a8-dijkstra.summary: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest route from one source to every vertex when no edge has a negative weight, by always finalising the closest vertex not yet finalised. You will learn why that greedy choice is correct, how to implement it with a priority queue, an ordered set or a plain array, how to print the path, why negative edges break it, and how to pick the right shortest-path algorithm — including Dial's bucket queue and the D'Esopo-Pape deque method.

a8-euler-path.summary: An Euler path uses every edge of a graph exactly once, and an Euler circuit does so and returns to its start. You will learn the simple degree test that decides whether one exists, how Hierholzer's algorithm builds one in linear time, why Fleury's bridge-avoiding method is slower, how directed graphs differ, and how the Chinese Postman problem extends the idea to routes that must repeat some edges.

a8-floyd-warshall.summary: Floyd-Warshall computes the shortest distance between every pair of vertices with three nested loops, by letting paths use one more allowed "via" vertex at a time. You will learn why its loop order is fixed, how it handles negative edges and cycles, and the related techniques for all-pairs and special-structure shortest paths — Johnson's algorithm, multistage graphs, 0-1 weighted graphs and the minimum mean cycle.

a8-gfg-must-do-extras.summary: GeeksforGeeks-style "must-do" graph lists mix famous problems with a few that do not fit the usual chapters. This lesson maps every common one to the pattern and lesson that solves it, then teaches the ones that need their own explanation — minimum swaps to sort as cycles of a permutation, minimum cost path as Dijkstra on a grid, and the shortest chain of one-letter word changes with one- and two-sided BFS.

a8-graph-coloring.summary: Graph colouring assigns colours to vertices so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour — the model behind timetables, register allocation and frequency assignment. You will learn why two colours are easy but three are NP-complete, how to decide m-colourability by backtracking, how greedy and DSatur heuristics behave, and three classic companions — the Traveling Salesman Problem, the Erdős–Rényi random graph and the Petersen graph.

a8-graph-interview-framework.summary: Most graph interview problems never say "graph". This lesson gives you a repeatable way to solve them — decide what the vertices and edges are, read the question and the constraints to pick an algorithm, then avoid the handful of mistakes that sink most attempts — and it ties every earlier graph lesson into one map you can revise from.

a8-graph-representation.summary: A graph is a set of things plus the connections between them, and before any graph algorithm can run you must choose how to store those connections in memory. You will learn the vocabulary of graphs, the three standard representations and their costs, how to pick one from a problem's constraints, and two classic representation problems — reachability for every pair (transitive closure) and building a graph from a list of degrees.

a8-max-flow.summary: Maximum flow asks how much can be pushed from a source to a sink through a network whose edges have capacities. You will learn the residual graph and augmenting paths, why the maximum flow always equals the minimum cut, the main algorithms (Ford-Fulkerson, Edmonds-Karp, Dinic, push-relabel), and how matching, disjoint paths, channel assignment and global min cut reduce to flows and cuts.

a8-mst-kruskal.summary: A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex of a weighted graph using the cheapest possible set of edges. You will learn why greedy choices are safe here (the cut and cycle properties), how Kruskal's algorithm uses sorting and Union-Find, how Prim's algorithm grows one tree with a priority queue, and the wider family — Borůvka, reverse-delete, counting spanning trees, minimum-product trees and the real systems that rely on MSTs.

a8-multi-source-bfs.summary: Multi-source BFS finds, for every cell or vertex, the distance to the nearest of many starting points in a single breadth-first pass. Around it sits the whole family of grid and state-space BFS problems — flood fill, islands, rotting oranges, word ladders, water jugs, 0-1 BFS — which all come down to modelling the problem as a graph and choosing the right traversal.

a8-scc.summary: A strongly connected component is a largest group of vertices in a directed graph where every vertex can reach every other. You will learn why these groups exist, how Kosaraju's and Tarjan's algorithms find all of them in linear time, how collapsing them turns any directed graph into a DAG, and how the same ideas solve 2-SAT, walk counting and the word-circle puzzle.

a8-topological-sorting.summary: A topological sort lists the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that every edge points forward, which is exactly the order in which dependent tasks can be done. You will learn Kahn's algorithm and the DFS finishing-time method, how to use them for course schedules and dependency ordering, how to enumerate every valid order, and how a topological order turns shortest paths, longest paths and many dynamic programs on DAGs into a single linear pass.

a8-union-find.summary: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) keeps elements in groups that can be merged, and answers "are these two in the same group?" in effectively constant time. You will learn how a forest of parent pointers represents the groups, why path compression and union by rank or size make it fast, and how to apply it to grids, streams of edges and offline connectivity queries.

a9-combination-sum.summary: Combination Sum asks for every group of numbers that adds up to a target. You will learn how one index decides between reuse and single use, why sorting turns an overshoot into an early stop, how to skip duplicate values safely, and how to recognise when the question really wants a count — which is a dynamic programming problem, not a backtracking one.

a9-combinations.summary: A combination is a choice of k items from n where order does not matter, and there are C(n, k) of them. You will learn to generate them with the start-index backtracking template, prune branches that cannot reach size k, handle repeated values, and tell combinations apart from subsets, permutations and cartesian products.

a9-constraint-backtracking.summary: Constraint-based backtracking fills in a solution one decision at a time and refuses any choice that already breaks a rule, so whole families of hopeless assignments are never generated. You will learn to model a problem as variables, domains and constraints, check those constraints incrementally in O(1), and speed the search up with variable ordering (MRV) and forward checking — the ideas behind Sudoku, N-Queens and graph-colouring solvers.

a9-grid-search.summary: Grid search backtracking explores paths through a 2D board one cell at a time, marking each cell while it is on the current path and releasing it when the search backs out. You will learn the mark–explore–unmark template through Word Search, see exactly why the unmark matters, count and list paths, scale to many words with a trie, and know when BFS, flood fill or DP is the better tool.

a9-n-queens.summary: N-Queens asks for every way to place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that none attacks another. It is the classic constraint-satisfaction problem; you will learn how placing one queen per row shrinks the search, how two simple formulas make every conflict check O(1), how a bitmask version speeds it up, and why pruning turns billions of candidate boards into about two thousand steps.

a9-permutations.summary: A permutation is one ordering of a collection, and n distinct items have n! of them. You will learn to generate every ordering with backtracking in two styles, avoid repeated orderings when values repeat, step to the next ordering without recursion, and jump straight to the k-th ordering — and why factorial growth limits all of this to small n.

a9-pruning.summary: Pruning stops a backtracking search from exploring branches that provably cannot contain a valid or better answer. You will learn the one rule every prune must obey, the five prunes that cover most problems — remaining count, sorted break and sum bounds, duplicate skipping, symmetry breaking and branch and bound — and how to measure what each one saves.

a9-subsets.summary: Generating every subset of a collection is the simplest backtracking problem and the template for most of the others. You will learn to see it as a tree of decisions, write it three different ways, handle duplicate values without producing repeated subsets, and explain exactly why it costs O(n · 2ⁿ).

b1-abort-controller-js.summary: Promises cannot be cancelled, so JavaScript platforms provide a separate cancellation token, AbortController and its AbortSignal. You will learn how the pair works, how to pass a signal through async code, how to make your own functions cancellable, and how timeouts and combined signals are built on the same mechanism.

b1-arithmetic-operators.summary: JavaScript's arithmetic operators look like a calculator's, but they first convert their operands, follow IEEE 754 floating-point rules, and treat `+` as both addition and string concatenation. You will learn exactly what each operator does, why `'20' + 5` is `'205'` while `'20' - 5` is `15`, and how to write arithmetic that stays correct with user input, negatives, money and BigInt.

b1-array-basics.summary: A JavaScript array is an ordered, zero-indexed list — but underneath it is an ordinary object with numeric-string keys and a self-maintaining `length`. You will learn how to create arrays without traps, how indexing and `length` really behave, and how "holes" in sparse arrays make some methods skip elements that others visit.

b1-array-from-isarray.summary: `Array.isArray` is the one reliable way to ask \"is this value an array?\", and `Array.from` turns anything list-shaped — strings, Sets, Maps, `arguments`, DOM `NodeList`s, generators, objects with a `length` — into a real array. You will learn what each one checks or copies, how `Array.of` fixes the `Array(3)` trap, and which tool to reach for when converting data.

b1-array-map-filter-reduce.summary: `map`, `filter` and `reduce` turn the three most common loops — transform every element, keep some elements, combine all elements into one value — into named, chainable operations. You will learn exactly how each one works, how `forEach`, `flat` and `flatMap` fit beside them, and the traps around return values, initial values, `async` callbacks and holes.

b1-array-mutation.summary: Some array methods change the array you call them on; others leave it alone and return a new one. You will learn which is which, what each one returns, how `push`/`pop`/`shift`/`unshift` and `slice`/`splice` behave at their edges, and how to update arrays without mutation — the skill that React state and other shared data depend on.

b1-array-search.summary: Searching an array means answering one of four questions — is it there, where is it, which element matches, or do any or all match. You will learn which method answers each question, the equality rule each one uses, what they return when nothing is found, and when a linear search should be replaced by a `Set` or `Map`.

b1-array-sort.summary: `sort` reorders an array in place, and by default it compares elements as strings — which is why `[10, 2, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 2]`. You will learn how to write comparator functions for numbers, strings, dates and objects, how to sort by several keys, what stability guarantees, and when to use the copying `toSorted` instead.

b1-arraybuffer.summary: An ArrayBuffer is a fixed block of raw bytes, and typed arrays and DataView are the "views" that read and write those bytes as integers or floating-point numbers. You will learn how buffers and views share memory, how byte order works, and how to parse and build binary formats such as file headers and network messages.

b1-arrow-functions.summary: Arrow functions — `(a, b) => a + b` — are a compact function syntax with one big behavioural difference, they take `this` from the surrounding code instead of from how they are called. You will learn every syntax form, what arrows deliberately lack (`this`, `arguments`, `new`, `prototype`), how lexical `this` fixes lost-`this` bugs in callbacks, and when an arrow is the wrong choice.

b1-assignment-operators.summary: Assignment operators write a value into a variable or property. You will learn what can appear on the left of `=`, why assignment is itself an expression, how compound operators like `+=` read and write the target exactly once, and how logical assignment (`||=`, `&&=`, `??=`) can skip the write entirely.

b1-async-await.summary: async/await lets you write Promise-based code that reads top to bottom like ordinary synchronous code. You will learn exactly what the two keywords do, how an async function is suspended and resumed through the microtask queue, how errors flow through try/catch, and why waiting with await never freezes the page or the server.

b1-async-control-flow.summary: Real features are workflows of many asynchronous steps — some dependent, some independent, some optional, some repeated. This lesson teaches the patterns for sequencing, fanning out, joining, branching, looping, polling and retrying with async/await, and how to choose between them for speed and correct error handling.

b1-async-debugging.summary: Asynchronous bugs are rarely about one wrong line; they are about callbacks running in an order you did not expect. You will learn why an ordinary stack trace loses the history of async code, how async stack traces and promise-rejection breakpoints recover it, and how to diagnose stale responses, unhandled rejections and misleading timings.

b1-autoboxing.summary: Primitives such as strings and numbers have no properties of their own, yet `'hi'.toUpperCase()` works. You will learn how JavaScript briefly wraps a primitive in a wrapper object to look up a property, why anything you store on that wrapper disappears, and why you should never create wrapper objects yourself with `new`.

b1-basic-debugging.summary: Debugging is a repeatable method for finding out why a program does something other than what you intended — reproduce the problem, observe real values, form a hypothesis, test it, and fix the cause. You will learn to read JavaScript error messages and stack traces, use logging deliberately, pause code with breakpoints and the `debugger` statement, and narrow down a bug instead of guessing.

b1-bigint.summary: BigInt is JavaScript's primitive for whole numbers of any size. You will learn how to create bigints safely, how their arithmetic differs from number arithmetic, why they refuse to mix with numbers, and how to move them through JSON, typed arrays and APIs — ending with decoding real 64-bit snowflake IDs.

b1-bitwise-operators.summary: JavaScript's bitwise operators work on the individual binary digits of a number, but only after converting it to a 32-bit integer. You will learn what each operator does, exactly how that conversion truncates and wraps values, how to use bit flags safely, and when `BigInt`, `Math.imul` or typed arrays are the better tool.

b1-blob-file-js.summary: A Blob is an immutable chunk of bytes with a MIME type, and a File is a Blob with a name and a modification time. You will learn how to create, slice and read them with the promise-based methods and streams, how they differ from ArrayBuffers and strings, and why the older FileReader API still appears in code you maintain.

b1-break-continue.summary: `break` ends a loop or `switch` early and `continue` skips to the next iteration. You will learn exactly where each one sends execution in every kind of loop, how they interact with `switch` and `finally`, why they cannot cross a function boundary (so they do not work inside `forEach`), and how labels let them target an outer loop.

b1-call-stack.summary: The call stack is how a JavaScript engine keeps track of which function is running and where to go back to when it finishes. You will learn to trace pushes and pops by hand, see what a stack frame holds, understand why deep recursion throws a RangeError, and read a stack trace to find where a bug really is.

b1-call.summary: The methods `call`, `apply` and `bind` let you choose the value of `this` for a function instead of leaving it to the call site. You will learn what each one does, how they differ (run now with a list, run now with an array, or return a new function for later), how to use them to borrow methods and keep callbacks attached to their objects, and how they work well enough to implement them yourself.

b1-callback-concept.summary: A callback is a function you hand to other code so that it can call you back — now, later, once or many times. You will learn what makes a function a callback, the contract every callback API carries, the difference between synchronous and asynchronous callbacks, and the error-first convention that Node.js built its I/O on.

b1-callback-hell.summary: Callback hell is what asynchronous code turns into when every step must nest inside the previous step's callback, and inversion of control is the deeper problem of handing your continuation to code you do not control. You will learn to recognise both, flatten callback code without any library, and see exactly which problems promises and async/await solve.

b1-class-inheritance.summary: Inheritance lets one class reuse and specialise another through `extends`, with `super` giving access to the parent's constructor and methods. You will learn the two prototype links `extends` creates, why `super()` must run before `this`, how method overriding and dynamic dispatch work, and when inheritance is the wrong tool.

b1-classes-vs-factories.summary: JavaScript gives you three ways to produce many similar objects — constructor functions, classes and factory functions. You will learn exactly how they differ in method sharing, memory, privacy, instanceof, this-safety and the role of new, so that you can choose one deliberately and defend the choice in an interview.

b1-classes.summary: A JavaScript class is a compact way to write a constructor function and the shared prototype its objects delegate to. You will learn what the class syntax creates in memory, how construction runs, where instance and static members live, and how public and private fields change what an object exposes.

b1-closure-memory.summary: A closure keeps its captured variables alive for as long as the function itself can be reached, which is usually what you want and occasionally a memory leak. You will learn exactly what a closure retains, why closures from the same scope can keep each other's data alive, the leak patterns that appear in long-running apps, and how to find and fix them.

b1-closure-puzzles.summary: Closure interview puzzles test whether you can simulate JavaScript's scopes and timing in your head rather than recall memorised answers. You will learn a four-question method for solving any closure puzzle and apply it to the patterns interviewers use most — shared and per-iteration bindings, factories, shadowing, getters, parameter scopes, this, and async timing.

b1-closures-in-loops.summary: When you create functions inside a loop, each function closes over the loop's variables — and whether those variables are shared or fresh on every iteration decides what the functions see later. You will learn exactly how var, let and const behave in each kind of loop, why the famous setTimeout loop prints 3, 3, 3, and every correct way to fix it.

b1-closures.summary: A closure is a function together with the variables from the place where it was created, which it can keep reading and changing long after that place has finished running. You will learn how closures arise from lexical scope, what the engine keeps alive for them, and how to use them for private state, factories and callbacks.

b1-comparison-operators.summary: The relational operators `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` answer "which comes first?", but in JavaScript the answer depends on the operand types — two strings are compared character by character, everything else is converted to numbers, and `NaN` makes every comparison false. You will learn the exact algorithm, why `'10' < '9'` is `true`, why `null >= 0` is `true` while `null == 0` is `false`, and how to compare numbers, strings, dates and versions correctly.

b1-concurrency-limiting.summary: Running every async task at once with Promise.all is fast for ten items and dangerous for ten thousand. This lesson shows how to cap the number of tasks in flight — with batches, a worker pool, or a reusable limiter — how to keep results in order and slots from leaking on errors, and how to choose the limit.

b1-const.summary: const declares a block-scoped binding that must be given a value immediately and can never be pointed at a different value. You will learn exactly what const does and does not protect, how to make objects genuinely read-only when you need to, and why "const by default" is the modern rule.

b1-constructor-functions.summary: A constructor function is an ordinary function that, when called with `new`, produces objects sharing one prototype. You will learn how to write one, exactly what `new` does in four steps, what the `constructor` property is and is not, and how this pre-class pattern maps onto the `class` syntax you write today.

b1-copying-arrays.summary: `const b = a` does not copy an array, and `[...a]` copies only the outer list — the objects inside are still shared. You will learn the difference between a reference, a shallow copy and a deep copy, which copying technique to use, how each one treats holes, extra properties and subclasses, and how to copy nested arrays without surprises.

b1-copying-objects.summary: Copying an object in JavaScript can mean three very different things — copying the reference, copying one level, or copying the whole tree. You will learn what spread, Object.assign, structuredClone and the JSON round trip each really copy, why shallow copies share nested objects, and how to choose the right technique for state updates, snapshots and data sent between threads.

b1-currying.summary: Currying turns a function of several arguments into a chain of functions that each take one, and partial application fixes some arguments now and leaves the rest for later. You will learn how both work through closures, how to write a generic curry and where it breaks, and how compose and pipe chain small functions into readable data pipelines.

b1-custom-errors.summary: Custom errors are your own subclasses of Error that name the failures of your application, so callers can recognise and handle them without parsing messages. You will learn how to write them correctly, carry extra data and causes, design a small hierarchy, and keep them working across transpilers, realms and the network.

b1-date-basics.summary: A JavaScript `Date` is a mutable object holding one number — milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC — with methods that read that moment either in UTC or in the computer's local time zone. You will learn how to create, read, copy, compare and validate dates, how Unix timestamps relate to that number, and why local time versus UTC is behind most date bugs.

b1-date-pitfalls.summary: Date arithmetic looks like adding numbers, but calendars have months of different lengths, leap years and daylight-saving jumps, and JavaScript's `Date` handles them by silently rolling over. You will learn the specific ways date math goes wrong — month overflow, DST gaps, off-by-one day counts, mutation, string sorting and invalid dates — and the correct pattern for each.

b1-debounce.summary: Debouncing delays a function until a burst of calls has gone quiet, so that a search box sends one request after the user stops typing instead of one per keystroke. You will learn how debounce works with timers and closures, implement it with leading, trailing, cancel and flush behaviour, and learn when to choose it over throttling.

b1-destructuring.summary: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays and properties from objects into variables with a pattern that mirrors the shape of the data. You will learn array and object patterns, defaults, renaming and nesting, how destructuring works in function parameters, and the exact rules that decide when it throws.

b1-devtools.summary: Browser DevTools let you look inside a running page — its live DOM, its console, its network traffic and its paused JavaScript. You will learn what each panel is for, how to pause code with breakpoints and step through it, and how to read the Scope, Watch and Call Stack panes so that debugging becomes observation instead of guessing.

b1-ecmascript.summary: ECMAScript is the standard that defines the JavaScript language, and "JavaScript" is the everyday name for engines that implement it plus whatever their host adds. You will learn who writes the standard, how new features move from idea to specification, what the edition names like ES6 and ES2020 mean, and how to ship modern syntax to environments that do not support it yet.

b1-equality.summary: JavaScript has several ways to ask "are these the same?" — strict `===`, loose `==`, their negations `!==` and `!=`, `Object.is`, and the rule that `Map`, `Set` and `includes` use internally. You will learn the exact algorithm behind each, why `[] == ![]` is true and `NaN === NaN` is false, why two identical-looking objects are never equal, and which comparison to reach for in real code.

b1-error-propagation.summary: An error in JavaScript travels along one of two channels — up the call stack as a thrown exception, or down a promise chain as a rejection — and `async`/`await` joins the two. You will learn exactly how each channel carries a failure, where errors escape both, and how to decide which layer of an application should catch, wrap, or rethrow.

b1-error-types.summary: JavaScript reports failures as error objects that belong to a small family of built-in types. You will learn what an error object contains, which language rule each built-in type stands for, and how to tell them apart reliably when you catch one.

b1-esm-vs-cjs.summary: JavaScript has two module systems in daily use — CommonJS, which Node.js built first, and the standard ES modules. You will learn how each one loads code, why ESM imports are live bindings while `require` hands you an object, how both handle circular dependencies, what top-level `await` does to a module graph, and why only ESM can be reliably tree-shaken.

b1-event-loop-puzzles.summary: Event-loop puzzles ask you to predict the order in which logs from synchronous code, promises, async functions and timers appear. You will learn a reliable step-by-step method for solving them on paper, practise it on ten puzzles of increasing difficulty, and learn to explain each answer the way interviewers want to hear it.

b1-event-loop.summary: The event loop is the scheduler that decides when each piece of JavaScript runs on a single thread — your script, promise callbacks, timers, clicks and network responses. You will learn its exact steps, why a promise callback beats a zero-millisecond timer, why long synchronous work freezes a page, and how browsers and Node.js differ.

b1-execution-contexts.summary: An execution context is the record the JavaScript engine keeps for one running piece of code — which variables exist, what `this` is, and where to look for names it does not own. You will learn how a context is created and then executed, how the global and function contexts differ, and how their environments explain hoisting, scope and closures as one mechanism.

b1-explicit-conversion.summary: Explicit conversion is turning a value into a string, number or boolean on purpose, at a point you choose, instead of letting an operator guess. You will learn exactly what `String()`, `Number()`, `Boolean()`, `parseInt`, `parseFloat` and unary `+` do with every kind of input, where each one surprises people, and how to convert untrusted input safely at the edges of a program.

b1-first-class-functions.summary: In JavaScript, functions are values — you can store them, pass them to other functions and return them from functions. You will learn what "first-class" means, how higher-order functions such as map, filter and addEventListener use this, how to write your own function factories and wrappers, and how callbacks work, including the difference between synchronous and asynchronous ones.

b1-for-loops.summary: Loops repeat code until a condition says stop. You will learn exactly how JavaScript's three classic loops — `for`, `while` and `do...while` — execute, how `let` gives each iteration of a `for` loop its own variable, and how to avoid the off-by-one errors, infinite loops and mutation bugs that cause most loop failures.

b1-for-of-in.summary: JavaScript has two loops that look almost identical but walk completely different things. `for...of` walks the values an iterable produces; `for...in` walks the enumerable string keys of an object, including inherited ones. You will learn the protocol behind each, why `for...in` is the wrong tool for arrays, and which loop or `Object` method to reach for in every common situation.

b1-function-declaration.summary: A function declaration — `function name(params) { body }` — creates a named, reusable function that exists from the moment its scope is entered. You will learn its syntax and parts, how calling and returning work, why declarations can be called before their line, and the block-scoping rules that differ between strict and sloppy code.

b1-function-expression.summary: A function expression creates a function as a value, at the moment the expression runs, so you can store it in a variable, pass it to another function or choose it at runtime. You will learn how it differs from a declaration, why it cannot be called before its line, and how named and anonymous function expressions affect recursion, stack traces and the function's name property.

b1-function-hoisting.summary: The same function can be written as a declaration or as an expression, and the two behave differently if you call them before the line that defines them. You will learn exactly what each form looks like before its line runs, how to read the three different errors you can get, and how to choose a style deliberately.

b1-functional-style.summary: The same program can be written as step-by-step instructions that change variables (imperative) or as a description of the result built from transformations (declarative). You will learn how the two styles differ in JavaScript, when each reads better, and how immutability — producing new values instead of editing old ones — makes the declarative style safe in UI code.

b1-garbage-collection.summary: Garbage collection is how a JavaScript engine finds unreachable objects and reuses their memory without stopping your page for long. You will learn why engines trace from roots instead of counting references, how mark-and-sweep and generational collection work, and what that means for the code you write.

b1-getters-setters.summary: Getters and setters are accessor properties — properties that run a function when they are read or assigned, while still looking like ordinary fields to the code that uses them. You will learn the syntax in object literals, classes and Object.defineProperty, where the real value is stored, how accessors interact with inheritance, copying and JSON, and when an explicit method is the better choice.

b1-global-variables.summary: A global variable is a name that every script in a realm can see, and `globalThis` is the one portable way to reach the object that holds many of them. You will learn every way a global gets created, why the global scope is split into two stores, how browsers, workers and Node.js differ, and why modern code keeps its own names out of the global scope.

b1-hoisting-puzzles.summary: Hoisting puzzles are short programs whose output looks wrong until you apply the creation phase. You will learn a two-pass method for solving any of them and work through the patterns interviewers use — var shadowing, var and function name clashes, function expressions, the temporal dead zone, default parameters, block-level functions and classes.

b1-hoisting.summary: Hoisting is the name for a simple fact with surprising consequences — JavaScript sets up every declaration in a scope before running any of the scope's code. You will learn the two phases behind it, exactly what each kind of declaration (var, function, let, const, class, import) looks like before its line runs, and how to read code the way the engine does.

b1-if-else.summary: The `if` statement is how a JavaScript program chooses between paths. You will learn exactly how its condition is tested (truthiness, not `=== true`), why `else if` is not a separate keyword, how braces and block scope change behaviour, and how to structure decisions so they stay readable as they grow.

b1-iife.summary: An Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE) is a function that is created and called in the same breath, so its body runs once inside a private scope. You will learn why the strange parentheses are required, how IIFEs gave JavaScript private state and modules before the language had them, and where they are still the right tool today.

b1-impl-call-apply-bind.summary: Re-implementing `call`, `apply` and `bind` without using them forces you to understand how JavaScript decides `this` for a method call. You will build all three, see exactly where the classic "temporary property" trick differs from the real methods, and make your `bind` support partial arguments and `new`.

b1-impl-curry-compose.summary: `curry`, `compose` and `pipe` are the small functional-programming tools behind point-free code, Redux middleware and RxJS operators. You will implement each from closures and `reduce`, understand why `curry` depends on `fn.length` and when that breaks, and learn when these tools make code clearer and when they make it harder to read.

b1-impl-debounce-throttle.summary: Debounce, throttle and memoize are the three function wrappers every frontend engineer is asked to write. Each is a closure that remembers a little state — a timer, a timestamp or a cache — and decides whether to call the real function. You will build all three from scratch, add the options interviewers ask about (leading and trailing calls, cancel, custom cache keys), and learn where each one breaks.

b1-impl-deep-clone.summary: Deep clone, flatten and deep equality are three recursive walks over nested data — the same traversal with a different job at each node. You will implement all three by hand, handle cycles, shared references, dates, maps and sets, and learn exactly where `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` and `structuredClone` fall short.

b1-impl-event-emitter.summary: An event emitter lets one part of a program announce "this happened" while any number of other parts react, without either side knowing about the other. You will build one from scratch — `on`, `off`, `once`, `emit` — and learn the details that separate a toy from a correct implementation, such as snapshotting listeners during `emit`, function identity, error handling and leaks.

b1-impl-get-path.summary: A `get(object, path, defaultValue)` helper reads a deeply nested value such as `'orders[0].items[0].qty'` without crashing when something along the way is missing. You will build one from scratch — a path parser, a safe walk and a precise default rule — and learn why the same parsing code becomes a security hole when it is reused to write values.

b1-impl-lru.summary: A Least Recently Used (LRU) cache keeps a fixed number of entries and, when full, throws away the one that has gone unused the longest. You will implement it in JavaScript twice — with the insertion order of `Map`, and with the classic hash map plus doubly linked list — and learn why both give O(1) `get` and `set`.

b1-impl-map-filter-reduce.summary: Writing `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and `forEach` yourself is a classic interview exercise because each is a small loop with precise rules about callbacks, `thisArg`, holes and the starting accumulator. You will build all four from a plain `for` loop, match the behaviour the ECMAScript specification describes, and learn which details interviewers probe.

b1-impl-promise-combinators.summary: Implementing `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled` and `Promise.race` from scratch shows whether you understand how promises settle, why results must be stored by index, and what happens to the promises that lose. You will build all three (plus `Promise.any`), match the built-ins on edge cases such as empty input and non-promise values, and learn the bugs interviewers look for.

b1-impl-promise.summary: Building your own Promise class is the most thorough way to understand what `then`, chaining and `await` really do. You will implement one step by step — states, the executor, asynchronous handlers, chaining, thenable adoption, `catch` and `finally` — and check its behaviour against the native Promise.

b1-impl-retry-sleep.summary: Three small promise utilities show up in almost every production codebase and in many interviews — `sleep`, `retry` with exponential backoff, and a concurrency limiter. You will build each one from scratch, make them cancellable with `AbortSignal`, and learn the details that decide whether they help a struggling system or make it worse.

b1-in-delete-void.summary: `in`, `delete`, `void` and `instanceof` are JavaScript's keyword operators: they test whether a property exists, remove a property, discard a value, and check an object's prototype chain. You will learn exactly what each one checks or changes, the surprises around inherited properties, arrays, strict mode and primitives, and the modern alternatives you should often reach for instead.

b1-instanceof.summary: The `instanceof` operator answers "is this object a kind of X?" by searching the object's prototype chain for `X.prototype`. You will learn the exact algorithm, why it returns surprising answers for primitives, values from other realms and objects whose prototype was changed, how `Symbol.hasInstance` customises it, and which check to use instead when `instanceof` is the wrong tool.

b1-intl-datetime.summary: `Intl.DateTimeFormat` turns an instant into text a person in a particular language and time zone expects to read. You will learn how locales and options control the output, how to show any IANA time zone, how `formatToParts` and `formatRange` give you structured and range output, and why formatted strings are for display only.

b1-iterators.summary: Iterators are the one protocol behind `for...of`, spread, destructuring, `Map`, `Set` and streaming data in JavaScript. You will learn how the protocol works, how to make your own objects iterable, how generators write iterators for you, and how async iterators walk data that arrives over time.

b1-js-engine.summary: A JavaScript engine is the program that turns your source code into running behaviour — it parses, compiles and executes code, keeps the call stack, and manages memory on a garbage-collected heap. You will learn what an engine does and does not do, how it differs from the browser or Node.js that hosts it, and how the heap holds your objects and closures.

b1-js-oop-principles.summary: Encapsulation, polymorphism and composition are the design ideas that keep object-based code changeable as it grows. You will learn what each one means in JavaScript specifically — where they come from closures, private fields, prototype lookup and plain object references — and how to choose composition or inheritance for a real design.

b1-json-replacer-reviver.summary: `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse` accept hooks that let you decide how each value is written and rebuilt: a replacer and `toJSON` on the way out, a reviver on the way in. You will learn the exact order in which they run, what `this` and the key are at each call, and how to use them for redaction, dates, `BigInt`, `Map`/`Set` and class instances without corrupting data.
